If you like 1984 by George Orwell, if the intelligence services attract your attention, if you love the government, if you hate it, if you want a game with an original, creative and extremely immersive interface, if you need a completely exciting game: then, this is what you need. Orwell is extremely immersive, it starts looking like a simple hacking game, but when it develops you end fucked up.
Storyline had been interesting and intriguing. If you like a good story this would be nice.

Because of the recent announcement of facial recognition tech in London, this game is suddenly more topical. It's a fun and interesting take on the age of surveillance with a compelling story to make you think about the pros and cons of surveillance for justice.

It was simple and easy to understand and play with a fairly smooth UI. The main issue was I think an illusion of choice; I often times I had to choose info I didn't want to (incriminating, vague, or easily misinterpreted "evidence") in order for the story to progress.

However it was fun, engaging and could really draw you in for a few hours at a time. I think the message of this game is very important, though not particularly groundbreaking. I'm probably going to replay for achievements and to see how much my actions actually affect the outcome of the story. The sequel is also sitting in my library and I can't wait to see how the story has progressed.

You are a goverment investigator that uses a data analysis inteligent OS to investigate the citizen of a dystopian foreign country. The plot has some weak spots, but I found the game satisfaying and interesting enough. You have to go through social media, news, blogs and even personal computers or phones of the "suspects" in order to find the perpetuator of some terrorist attack. The game plays with the limits between privacy and security, fake news, power, etc...

The mechanics are simple, you just select pieces of information and link them with a suspect, but you can choose wrong information and change the narrative of the investigation (you are the only one that has acces to the OS), this opens the game to some really interesting stuff.

While the concept of the game is interesting I think it's not executed very well. Often times the game gets into a state where you can't collect any more information and you need to provide the surveillance system with data that you found. But there would often be two conflicting datasets, usually diametrically opposite, available for upload but you have no real way of determining which one is true/false. So you end up just taking the best guess and then the game starts playing this dramatic music because it's exactly at that point that somebody has to suddenly make a phone call or send an email with some sort of a revelation. Needless to say most of the time it doesn't land for me. My reaction to these situations would mostly be: "Oh, ok. I guess that's what happened.". The game goes out of its way to put you in a dead-end situation that could go either way and then it tries to make a tense situation out of it. It doesn't really work for me and I felt like the writing wasn't very strong in general. Especially when it comes to one character that communicates directly with you and beats you over the head with expository information and game tips in a way that attempts to be subtle but isn't really.

A fun little document reading simulator.

Seriously, that is the gameplay. It's like a season of 24, where you have to find out where the bomb is going to go off, and it's all up to you, but instead of an elite anti-terrorist agent, you're some rando sitting in front of a PC, hired to sift through documents. That is literally who you are, in the universe of the game. You submit portions of documents to the system, and this unlocks more documents. That may sound a little silly, but the game explains itself pretty well.

No need to worry about 'pixel hunting' or broken logic - all problems are solved and the plot is progressed in all cases by finding the right entry in the right document. If anything, the game holds your hand. 

You can only submit portions of any document that the system deems potentially relevant. You cannot get a game over - you could play this game through by blindly submitting every bit of highlighted text you found, without paying attention to the plot.

But the plot itself is worth paying attention to - a slow-burn story of a parallel world with technology from five minutes into the future. That lawyer guy on youtube who rates the legal accuracy of various pieces of pop culture would probably not rate this thing too highly. But it is fun, and the rationale for everything that happens is internally consistent.

There are branching paths and different outcomes to minor plot points, as well as alternate endings, depending on how you play  - which boils down to which pieces of information you choose to submit or not submit. It is worth the second and even third play-throughs needed to explore every possible outcome.

Which brings me to my two main complaints:

- There is a checkpoint system, limited to the five main chapters/days of the campaign. You can replay a previous day/chapter, but as soon as you start say, chapter two, your progress in the remaining 3 chapters is lost.

- There is no fast-track buttons for voice or text conversations - they play out in real time, complete with 'realistic' pauses, whether you like it or not.

Neither of these are game-breaking, and are more just quality of life features that I found to be conspicuously absent. Their absence mean that secondary playthroughs for achievements/branch discovery take a little longer than they otherwise would.

I bought Orwell on sale, and went in to it without doing much homework, but I got the impression that this would be several distinct yet related cases. It's more like one big ongoing case. Also in contrast to the Ace Attorney games, which Orwell reminds me of just a little, the plot is a little more serious, and the characters a little less colorful. But if you like that series, or sifting through documents to find a terrorist in a dystopian alternate world sounds like fun to you, and if none of what I have written sounds like a deal-breaker, and you find this game at a price that you think is worth ten or so hours of gameplay, go for it.

One final thought - this game is about a surveillance state, but it doesn't take the easy way out. It poses the dilemma of government overreach/corruption for 'safety' vs. privacy/freedom concerns in an interesting way. I would not say that Orwell is quite as brilliant or profound as some of the glowing reviews suggest, but I do like the way that the plot, the gameplay, and the endings you are able to choose all come together to get you thinking about this issue, even if just a little.

"But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences."

The little details, including the occasional quote from 1984, as well as a meme or or advert on web sites are a nice touch.

One note, sometimes it can be frustrating to find the "trigger" for the next info reveal. It is also not just a game where you simply find info and add it to the Orwell database - you need to weigh the meaning/context of the data and decide what should be reported.

Due to several of the achievements being linked to the aforementioned branching paths, it would require a minimum of 3 plays, and you cannot restart from a previous save game to save time.

I've been hesitating writing a review for this one, as part of me likes the game but another part is very annoyed with it. After giving it some rest and extra thought, I have to downvote it.

The gameplay is fine, I actually quite liked that. The concept works and I would have loved a much more difficult version using this technique.

Sadly, the story is very flawed and made in such a way to get the game's "message" out. It is very biased towards why all this is a bad idea and pretty much gives no indication why and how it could actually work. And you know, that all would have been fine if done right, but everything in the story hinges on a lot of coincidences and it takes away from how an actual Orwell system could maybe properly work.

It still wouldn't, but this case does not show the actual flaws of such a system. And that is the problem of this game. It starts off by you following ONE suspect. In a true case you would have had information on everyone at the crime scene, and this is only the first big flaw why this is a bad representation of a system like this. [spoiler]And then that suspect ends up not being involved at all, but by coincidence she does happen to be in contact with the true criminal. Oh, sure, the writers eventually tried to make a link and explain it was the criminal who was responsible for the first suspect to be a the crime scene. Which ends up with the story making even less sense as there is absolutely no indication why the criminal would even want this suspect to be at the first crime scene.[/spoiler] And it just goes downhill from there, with more random stuff happening that just happens to be convenient for this poor mirror or a true spying system.

Conclusion: Good concept, but the writing keeps it from being a good game.

Orwell puts you in the position of a security agent digging through public and private information to uncover the truth. Or to pull everything out of context to fabricate a lie. Or to be honestly mistaken, and be responsible for the prosecution of innocent people. Your actions have consequences, so you are presented a constant ethical dilemma, and are second-guessing yourself on every plot-twist and turn as events unfold.

Its very well put together, multi-faceted story is extremely engaging, though told only through text and simple graphics. The replay value is however badly hurt by chats and phone calls going on in real-time, making you wait minutes on end through a conversation you already know before you finally have the possibility to explore another outcome.

All in all this game has made me feel like a creepy stalker, government disobeying rebel and unethical secret agent, It has made me laugh, shout in anger, feel defeated, and cheer in victory-- as well as making me more aware of the power of information and social media. Wholeheartedly recommended to anyone interested in story-driven dystopian games, investigation, manipulation, and Facebook conspiracists.

This game is a punch in the gut.

It gives you a slow lead in to a game and very quickly spirals into an uncontrollable tailspin of compounding decisions.

There are genuine heart-wrenching consequences to the actions you take if you choose wrong.

The game is a warning on the dangers that come with complete surveillance, how people can become collateral damage to someone thinking they have all the information to make an informed decision.

Regardless of what you do, in your quest to find "that guilty person" you will accidentally impact and potentially destroy the lives of so many other people.

It's such a simple game.  It's not difficult.  It's a game that makes you think about real life, about how our decisions can affect others.  It's a game that teaches you that there is always a "next step" when it comes to trying to attain complete safety for a society, and that trying for it can ultimately destroy the society and everything it stands for.

I bought this game as a bundle with Unheard, and ended up paying $1 at checkout for both of them - and I feel like I cheated the developer.  So rarely does a game come along and get across a message so well without doing it in an obvious way.

This game is a well written, thought provoking piece and I recommend it to anyone who is politically interested or just wants a good story to play through. The game has multiple endings and makes you feel like your actions have consequences on the lives of the characters you investigate which I think is an achievement. Actions with meaning add depth to the gameplay that would've otherwise been boring and menial. The ability to explore multiple endings gives it replay value for achievement hunters and people who want to see what would've happened if they did things differently. The main story, the ideas what come with it, and how it was delivered in the gameplay makes it hard not to recommend. 

P.S. There's a free demo that you can try out and if you like it and see the game on sale consider buying it.

Alright, I'll keep this as basic as I can so you know what you're getting yourself into.


[h1] The Story [/h1] 

First off, this is a spoiler free re-view, If you are looking for spoilers, please don't this game is depending on 
[b] ENTIRELY [/b]  on the story. That being said the story itself is brilliant. The characters are like-able (and quite the opposite as well), the plot unravels so well that you never know what happens next or what awaits you and the atmosphere of it all gets more and more intense as you progress. 

[h1] Game-play [/h1] 

There is not much to be said about game-play, it is fairly basic, but works incredibly well. Basic web-coordination and a little bit of memory/logical thinking will save you a lot of time. However, depending on [b] YOUR [/b] choices, some key parts of the story will change (There is no real ''answer'', most of the time going with your gut is the best you can do). In the end, your choices will impact the outcome, and the ending of the game itself.

[h1] Soundtrack [/h1] 

It started off very simple, generic investigation theme and yaddi yadda, you get the point. However, I soon found out that the music itself is very dynamic and will change depending on the situation you will find yourself in. Thanks to that little touch it kept me on the edge of my seat, and dropped my jaw when it was supposed to, great work, loved it.

[h1] Re-play ability [/h1] 

The game has multiple endings and some key factors change the story, so the way you play can be completely different from how another person would play. Other than that, once you complete the game, you know the story as well as the ''plot-twists'' that will appear, so you have the upper-hand, so to speak. 

[h1] Worth it ? [/h1] 

Absolutely ! The game is very short and as of the day of this re-view, it has one sequel. You can complete it in under 5 hours, for all achievements about 8-9 I wager. Although I recommend buying it while it is on sale and preferably in a bundle with the sequel. I would rate this game an 8/10, it is a really good game, but a bit too short for my liking.

It is amazing they way they gave me the sense of communicating with my "advisors" in the story, even though I could not type a line of text. Whenever I thought that there was a frustrating aspect to the game, I realized that my frustration was part of the storyline. This is an excellent design, flawless execution and riveting gameplay experience. I just hope my country, the U.S.A., doesn't have an extradition treaty with The Nation! I will be looking over my shoulder...
